activities.caption: Newtonian or non-Newtonian? file the fluids
activities.name: fmViscBuckets

config.prompt: Viscosity that stays constant, or structure that misbehaves — file each fluid:

items.label: blood — shear-thinning, red cells align at speed
paint — spreads under a brush, stays on the wall
ketchup — refuses to move until pushed hard enough
silly putty — bounces fast, flows slowly
cold crude oil behaving as a Bingham plastic

config.why: A pipeline design for water cannot be reused for sludge or cold crude — the Bingham plastic needs a starting pressure just to unstick.

activities.anchor: One non-obvious property rule shapes everything else
activities.caption: bet the wall velocity before the boundary layer
activities.name: fmNoSlipPredict

config.q: Water flows past a pipe wall. The water's velocity exactly at the surface is…
config.why: No-slip: velocity is exactly zero at the surface, rising to free-stream across the boundary layer — the millimetres-to-centimetres zone that carries essentially all the friction drag, most of the heat transfer, and (if it separates) the stall of wings.

activities.anchor: the historic way small towns ran mains pressure without a pump in sight
activities.caption: call the magnitude — pressure from height alone
activities.name: fmTowerEstimate

config.prompt: A water tower's free surface stands 30 m above the tap. Roughly what pressure does gravity alone deliver at the tap?
config.why: p = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 30 ≈ 294 kPa — about 3 bar from height alone.
config.context: A diver at 10 m feels one extra atmosphere (98 kPa) for exactly the same reason.

activities.anchor: violently turbulent, like virtually every industrial pipe
activities.caption: pin the Reynolds number on the scale
activities.name: fmRePlace

config.prompt: Re = ρvL/μ for water at 2 m/s in a 100 mm pipe — where does it land?
config.why: 1000 × 2 × 0.1 ÷ 0.001 = 200,000 — far past the ~4,000 where full turbulence is established; transition sits near 2,300. Two flows with the same Re behave the same way scaled, which is why a 1:50 spillway model can certify the full-size structure.

activities.caption: the famous wrong lift story — find the faulty line
activities.name: fmLiftSpot

config.prompt: A student explains aircraft lift. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: The top surface is curved, so air above has farther to travel
Equal transit time: both streams must arrive at the trailing edge together
So the air above must move faster over the top
Faster flow means lower pressure — and that is lift
Bernoulli is a bookkeeping identity along a streamline
config.correction: Aircraft fly fine with air arriving early on top — lift is a turning of the flow with pressure differences integrated over the surface.
config.why: The pressure drop is the energy that paid for the speed-up — a constriction accelerates the fluid, not the other way round.

activities.anchor: The pump pushing that water spends
activities.caption: fill the Darcy–Weisbach bill
activities.name: fmPipeCloze

config.text: Δp = f·(L/D)·(ρv²/2): with f ≈ %%0%%, (ρv²/2) = %%1%% Pa and L/D = %%2%%, the 100 m run loses about %%3%% kPa — and the pump spends roughly %%4%% W pushing the flow, about half a kilowatt of pure friction tax.
config.hint: One pipe size bigger halves the velocity — and quarters the loss, which is how the extra steel pays for itself in saved electricity.

activities.anchor: Where fast shallow flow meets slow deep flow
activities.caption: pair each instrument and phenomenon with its job
activities.name: fmMeterMatch

config.prompt: Flow measurement and free-surface phenomena — pair them:

pairs.right: pressure drop across a constriction — the orifice pays a permanent penalty
depth over a crest, mapped to discharge by a calibrated power law
open channels answering to gravity — n from 0.012 concrete to 0.035 weedy
energy dissipated violently on purpose — stilling basins protect the dam's toe

config.why: Ship designers know the Froude number as the wave-making tax: hull speed scales with √L — the reason long boats are fast boats.

activities.anchor: and why throttling with valves instead is thermodynamically silly
activities.caption: which curve is the pump's?
activities.name: fmCurveTrace

config.prompt: Head versus flow: one curve is the pump's characteristic, one is the system's. Which is the pump's?
config.why: Head delivered falls as flow rises; the system curve rises with its friction term — their crossing is where the physics puts the operating point, and series adds heads while parallel adds flows.
